title: How do you test with JUnit + Mockito? What are JUnit 5 lifecycle annotations? What is TDD vs BDD? What is @Mock vs @Spy? How do you verify interactions with ArgumentCaptor? What is code coverage (JaCoCo)? What is @SpringBootTest vs @WebMvcTest vs @DataJpaTest? Why test failure paths? What is unit vs integration vs contract vs E2E testing? When to use Testcontainers?
shortTitle: What are the Spring testing annotations?
keyPoints: Unit tests use Mockito (@Mock, @InjectMocks) with no Spring context and run in milliseconds
@WebMvcTest loads only the controller layer with MockMvc and mocked services for testing HTTP behavior
@DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer with an embedded or Testcontainers database for testing queries
@SpringBootTest loads the full application context for integration tests and is reserved for multi-layer testing
@Mock creates a full stub returning defaults; @Spy wraps a real object and calls real methods unless overridden
ArgumentCaptor captures arguments passed to mocks so you can assert on the exact values that were saved
Testcontainers spins up real Docker containers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) for tests, catching dialect-specific bugs

s1_definition.oneliner: Unit tests use Mockito with no Spring context for millisecond-fast testing, @WebMvcTest loads only the controller layer, @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer, and @SpringBootTest loads everything for full integration tests.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Unit test** – tests one class in isolation with Mockito mocks replacing all dependencies, no Spring context, runs in milliseconds.
- **@WebMvcTest** – loads only the web layer (controller, MockMvc, Jackson, validators, @ControllerAdvice) with all services mocked via @MockBean.
- **@DataJpaTest** – loads only the JPA layer (entities, repositories, EntityManager) with a test database, rolling back after each test.
- **@SpringBootTest** – loads the full application context for integration tests that exercise multiple layers together.
- **Testcontainers** – a library that spins up real Docker containers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) for tests and tears them down afterward.
- **@Mock vs @Spy** – @Mock returns defaults for all methods; @Spy wraps a real object and calls real methods unless explicitly overridden.
- **ArgumentCaptor** – captures the arguments passed to a mock's method so you can assert on the exact values.
s1_definition.analogy: Testing a National Bank of India branch at different levels. A unit test tests the teller's math with fake money and a fake vault (mocks). A @WebMvcTest tests the reception desk with a fake back office. A @DataJpaTest tests the vault with a real mini-vault (Testcontainers with PostgreSQL). A @SpringBootTest tests the entire branch with everything real, from the front door to the vault.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Testing in Spring Boot follows the testing pyramid. Unit tests with Mockito and no Spring context run in milliseconds and form the base. Rajesh writes them for every service class at National Bank of India using @Mock for dependencies, @InjectMocks for the subject, ArgumentCaptor for inspecting saved objects, and assertThatThrownBy for exception assertions. @WebMvcTest loads only the controller layer with MockMvc and mocked services, testing HTTP status codes, JSON structure, and validation without a database. @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer with Testcontainers providing a real PostgreSQL in Docker, testing queries, constraints, and migrations with the actual database dialect.

@SpringBootTest loads the full context for end-to-end integration tests and is reserved for scenarios that must exercise multiple layers together. Tests must cover failure paths equally: invalid input, missing data, duplicate records, unauthorized access, and timeouts. A transfer test that only checks the happy path will miss the bug where a negative amount passes validation.

Pankaj structures the test suite with a shared Testcontainers base class so PostgreSQL starts once and is reused across all repository tests. JaCoCo reports code coverage, but Pankaj reminds the team that coverage shows what ran, not whether the assertions are meaningful. A test with 100 percent coverage but no assertions proves nothing.

Remember one sentence: unit tests with Mockito for speed, @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest with Testcontainers for queries, and @SpringBootTest only when you need the full context.
